title: Emraan Hashmi Is Going Back to the Dark. 'Rooh' Drops Him Into a Musical-Horror Spectacle Built for the Big Screen.
excerpt: The man who made a generation flinch in the dark returns to the genre that built him — this time with songs, scale, and a 2027 release in three languages.
body:
There's a certain kind of Bollywood horror that belongs entirely to one face. Through the late 2000s and into the 2010s, if a film promised goosebumps and a chart-topping soundtrack in equal measure, the poster usually had **Emraan Hashmi** on it — brooding, haunted, soundtracked by a Pritam ballad you couldn't get out of your head. *Raaz: The Mystery Continues*, *Raaz 3*, *Ek Thi Daayan*. For a stretch there, he was the genre.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=ied8VS_PL8g</youtube>

Now he's coming back to it. The makers dropped the first-look title announcement this week with a line designed to crawl under your skin: *"You won't see it coming. You will feel it forever."* The film is called **Rooh** — Hindi for soul — and it is being sold as a high-concept musical-horror spectacle built, emphatically, for theatres.



> **"The "musical" half of the equation is the intriguing wager."**


> "Rooh is a film that immediately connected with me because it brings together new-age horror, emotion and music in a very powerful way. This is a space that audiences have always associated with me." — Emraan Hashmi


![The Mystery Continues — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/6/68/Raaz-The_Mystery_Continues_poster.jpg)


What makes this more than a nostalgia play is who's behind the camera. **Rooh** is directed by **Mayank Sharma**, the creator-director of Prime Video's *Breathe* franchise — a man with a real command of psychological dread, slow-burn atmosphere and characters who fall apart from the inside out. That's a meaningfully different instinct from the jump-scare-and-item-song school of Hindi horror. The screenplay is co-written by Sharma with **Vishal Kapoor**, who knows the territory cold from the chilling Marathi original *Lapachhapi* and its Hindi remake *Chhorii*. Between them, this is a horror pedigree that's earned, not borrowed.

The "musical" half of the equation is the intriguing wager. Emraan Hashmi horror was never just about fear; it was about the marriage of fear and melody — the reason those songs outlived the films. Reviving that formula for a 2027 audience raised on atmospheric, A24-adjacent dread is either a masterstroke or a misread, and we won't know which until we hear a single note. But the ambition is unmistakable. The makers, **Vikram Khakhar** and **Sunny Khanna** under the Vicked Films Productions banner, are pitching a visually rich, international-standard cinematic experience rather than a quick OTT horror flick.

Director Mayank Sharma framed his intent plainly. "Rooh is my attempt to create a film that goes beyond fear," he said. "It's emotionally layered and immersed with unsettling atmosphere and presented with contemporary cinematic treatment." That phrase — *beyond fear* — is the whole pitch. Horror that wants you to feel something other than your own pulse.

The timing is no accident. Bollywood horror is suddenly, improbably, hot again. Vikram Bhatt's *Haunted 3D: Echoes of the Past* turned into a surprise box-office winner, the top earner of its week at around Rs 16 crore, and Bhatt promptly announced *1920: Cold Winter* off the back of it. The genre that the industry had quietly written off as straight-to-streaming filler is back on theatre marquees — and Hashmi, who helped build that audience in the first place, is walking back in at exactly the right moment.

For the diaspora, the headline detail is the release strategy. **Rooh** is slated for a **2027 theatrical release** in **Hindi, Tamil and Telugu** — a three-language, pan-Indian rollout that signals real budget and real overseas intent. Multi-language horror travels unusually well in NRI markets, where a Friday-night fright film is one of the easiest sells across the US, UK, Canada and the Gulf. Expect a wide theatrical footprint when it lands, with a streaming window to follow.

There's a busy slate around this comeback, too. Hashmi will next be seen in **Awarapan 2**, the long-gestating sequel to his 2007 cult favourite, this time with Randeep Hooda, Disha Patani and Shabana Azmi in the mix. But it's **Rooh** that has the internet talking — because it's the one that sends him back into the dark, where, frankly, he's always been most magnetic. We've got a long wait until 2027. Consider the hook well and truly set.
